Since our signal the pair has kept climbing rather than fading: buys outnumber sells by more than two to one, hour volume comes to about 0.96x the market cap, and the token sits near its high.

created with AI with seedance 2.5 in @magnific

prompt used: photorealistic 20-second vertical 9:16 smartphone video filmed as one continuous handheld take on an iPhone 17 Pro 1x camera inside a real helicopter flying above an active volcano. 4K, 30fps, natural HDR, deep depth of field, constant helicopter vibration, micro-shake, autofocus/exposure breathing, realistic wind and rolling shutter. It must feel spontaneous, dangerous and real, never cinematic or CGI.

Use @image_start for the helicopter interior and opening composition: open rear cargo door, grey quilted metal interior, floor rails, red cargo netting, mountains outside. A huge 1m x 1m clear plastic bag completely filled with already-popped white/yellow popcorn sits centered on the floor. Keep the bag visually identical throughout.

CHARACTER LOCK: @image1 is the main character wearing a white T-shirt, grey shorts and white sneakers. His face, identity, hairstyle, skin tone, body proportions and clothing must remain identical in every frame. A second crew member assists.

0-4.3s: Start exactly like @image_start. The main character unclips the bag. Both men shout "Ready?!" "Yeah! Go!" "Push it, PUSH IT!" They struggle to shove the heavy bag toward the open door. Strong wind pushes it backward. It moves only inches per shove, plastic violently crinkling, popcorn shifting inside. His sneaker slips, he catches himself, then they finally push the bag out.

4.3-5.5s: Camera rushes to the doorway and tilts downward. The bag tumbles through the air toward the glowing volcanic crater.

5.5-8.8s: The bag hits molten lava and the plastic instantly vaporizes. Thousands of popcorn pieces explosively launch upward as one huge dense white column, matching @image_eruption, with glowing orange-red lava beneath. The character leans out, points downward and reacts in disbelief.

8.8-11s: Matching @image_return, the popcorn reaches helicopter altitude and becomes a massive horizontal storm blasting through the open door. Popcorn violently hits the character, cabin and camera. He shields his face as the camera jolts.

11-13.5s: The cabin is filled with swirling popcorn. The character is half-buried. He picks up one piece, eats it, chews twice, looks directly into camera and deadpans: "...it's warm."

13.5-16s: The second crew member bursts out laughing. Both laugh uncontrollably while popcorn swirls everywhere. Another gust blasts through the cabin. Camera shakes violently and the video ends abruptly mid-chaos.

PHYSICS: realistic heavy bag resistance, strong wind interaction, instant plastic vaporization, explosive unified popcorn column, horizontal return blast caused by wind/updraft, and popcorn swirling rather than falling straight down.

CAMERA: one continuous iPhone 17 Pro 1x handheld shot. No cuts, zooms, slow motion, gimbal stabilization, cinematic bokeh, lens flare or artificial lighting.

AUDIO: No music. Loud helicopter rotor, engine and wind throughout. Dialogue heavily muffled by rotor noise. Include plastic crinkling, grunts, volcanic WHUMP/BOOM, roaring rising popcorn, violent popcorn impacts, laughter and one audible crunch before "...it's warm."

No captions, logos, watermarks, overlays, UI or title cards.

Here’s how we avoid AI slop UI.

For the last couple of weeks, we’ve been testing different AI workflows while building Velox Themes 2.0.

What works best for us so far? We still design everything in Figma first, polish it until we’re happy with it, then let Codex or Claude handle the code.

From what we’ve tested, AI is really good at replicating a direction you give it. But when we ask it to come up with something fresh from scratch, we usually still need to step in and give it a strong creative direction.

That’s why I don’t think the creative part goes away with AI. Your ideas, taste, and creative direction still play a huge role.

AI just helps you build them much faster.

That’s also why we’re building a design library where you can find inspiration for your next website, then let your AI agent build it for you by copying the prompt or HTML.

items.text:
i pay $100/mo for claude max.

yesterday i read typesafe's launch post for jev, their new "system one" model. no chat, no free text. just typed structured decisions with calibrated probabilities. cant hallucinate because the output schema is fixed in advance.

thought that was a weird tradeoff at first.

then i saw the pricing and did the math out of pure curiosity.

$0.042 per million tokens in.
output is free. not cheap. free.

so $100 buys you ~2.4B tokens.

at ~2k tokens per decision (a normal medium-complexity workflow call) that's roughly 1.19 million decisions.

for the same $100 i pay for claude max, i get about 11,250 messages.

sat with that number for a minute.

that's 100x+ more units of work for identical money, just on a completely different category of work.

then i checked the speed.

same ~1.19M calls, run one at a time.

jev: ~23 hours, at 70ms per call.
a frontier llm doing that same volume: ~41 days on the fast end.
up to 12 years if you're stuck at the slow end of their 3 to 329 second range.

nobody runs a million calls sequentially in real life. but the per call ratio is the actual point. 40x to 200x faster depending on the task.

here's the honest part though.

jev doesn't chat. doesn't write code. doesn't reason out loud. zero free text, just probabilities against a schema you define upfront.

it's not replacing claude for me. i don't think it replaces claude for anyone doing real dev work.

what it's built for is the boring stuff buried in your app logic. classify this. route that. score this. extract that field. the smart if-statements every production system quietly depends on.

for that one slice, 100x cheaper and 40-200x faster isn't a marginal improvement. it's a different cost curve entirely.

still figuring out what this changes about how i'd architect a pipeline.

feels like the first real attempt at making "ai inside the hot path of your code" actually work, instead of being a slow expensive api call duct-taped onto the side of it.
